turns.doctor_question: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, yeah, thank you. Um, so I'm here because... well, it's been going on for a really long time, like months actually, and I just reached a point where I couldn't keep trying to just tough it out anymore. 

I'm taking some college classes right now, studying to be a radiologic tech, and between the long lectures and being in the actual radiology suite for clinicals, there is just so much sitting. And I mean, they expect you to just stay put and observe or listen to the instructor, but whenever I'm supposed to sit still like that, I swear I feel like I am literally crawling out of my skin. It's this intense, physical feeling, like my whole body is just... I don't know, it's like this pressure telling me to get up. 

I try so hard to just stay in the chair, I really do, but I always end up shifting my weight a million times, or I just straight up end up pacing in the back of the room. I'm constantly finding some excuse to move, you know? Like, I'll tell them, "Oh, I need to go check the lead aprons," or "Let me just grab a drink of water real quick," or I'll go to the bathroom three times in an hour just because if I don't get up and walk around, I feel like I'm going to explode. It's just so exhausting having to fight it every single day, and it's really starting to mess with my time in the suite.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they end up pacing in the back of the room and finding excuses to leave their seat, such as going to the bathroom multiple times, when they are expected to stay put.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an intense physical feeling of restlessness, stating they feel like they are 'crawling out of my skin' and 'going to explode' if they have to sit still.

turns.doctor_question: Are you currently taking any medications, including prescriptions or over-the-counter drugs?
turns.patient_response:
No, I'm not taking anything. Um, like, no prescriptions at all. I mean, my mom used to try and get me to take those daily multivitamin gummy things before I moved into the dorms, but honestly, I could never remember to take them. I'd always just be literally running out the door to get to my morning classes and totally forget they even existed. 

And as for over-the-counter stuff, not really that either. I mean, maybe an ibuprofen like once in a blue moon if I get a headache from staring at the monitors in the dark radiology rooms for too long, but even then, I usually just try to walk it off instead of taking a pill. I really don't like taking stuff, honestly. Even when I get a cold, I won't touch NyQuil or anything because I hate that heavy, stuck-in-bed feeling, you know? I'd rather just be up and moving, even if I feel like garbage. Oh, and I don't even drink coffee or energy drinks either, which all the other rad tech students basically live on, but I absolutely do not need them, I've got way too much energy as it is. So, yeah, I guess long story short, absolutely zero medications right now.

turns.doctor_question: Do you also find it difficult to pay attention or stay focused during your classes?
turns.patient_response:
Honestly, no, not really. I mean, the focusing part isn't the issue for me. Like, I hear everything the professors are saying, and I can totally follow along with the material. When we're going over anatomy or learning how to position a patient for a chest X-ray or whatever, my brain is completely locked in on the information. I get good grades on the quizzes, and I actually find the science behind it all super fascinating, so I don't zone out or get distracted by my phone or daydream or anything like that. 

It's literally just the sitting still part that kills me. My brain is paying attention, but my body is just screaming at me to move. Like, I'll be sitting there, absorbing every word about radiation safety protocols, but at the exact same time, my legs are bouncing up and down so fast the whole desk shakes, and I'm tapping my pen, and I'm twisting around in the chair trying to find a position where I don't feel like I'm trapped. Sometimes the instructors will even stop and ask me if I'm paying attention because I'm squirming around so much, and I can always repeat back exactly what they just said word for word, which usually surprises them. So yeah, my mind is completely focused, I just physically cannot keep my body in one spot while I'm doing it.

turns.doctor_question: Did you have this same kind of high energy and difficulty sitting still when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh man, yeah, absolutely. It’s definitely not just a recent thing, like, it didn't just start when I got into this radiology training or anything like that. Actually, my parents still talk about it all the time. They love bringing up my old elementary school parent-teacher conferences whenever family comes over, it's like their favorite story. 

It was literally the exact same conversation every single year, without fail. The teachers would sit them down and say how I was, you know, always out of my seat, pacing around the back of the classroom. And it wasn't just the standing up part, either. I was constantly calling out answers in the middle of class without raising my hand, or, um, like, if they were handing out an activity, I’d be rushing ahead and trying to do the whole thing before the teacher was even finished giving the directions. I just... I couldn't wait. I had to get it done right that second, I couldn't just sit there and listen to the instructions when the paper was right in front of me. 

I remember my mom used to try and make me run around the backyard in the mornings before the bus came just to tire me out, but it never really made a dent. So, yeah, this was all happening way, way before middle school even started. It's just always been who I am, I guess, just constantly buzzing and rushing through things since I was a little kid.

turns.doctor_question: Do you frequently misplace or lose things you need for school or daily life, like your keys, wallet, or assignments?
turns.patient_response:
Um, actually, no. That’s like the one thing I feel like I actually have totally under control. I mean, you’d think I would lose stuff all the time with how much I’m bouncing off the walls and rushing around, but I really don't. I have this, like, hyper-specific system for all my things. My keys, my wallet, my phone—they have exactly one place they are allowed to exist when they aren't in my hands. Like, the second I walk into my dorm, my keys go on this little magnetic hook by the door. Not on the desk, not on the bed, the hook. Every single time. 

And it’s the exact same thing at my clinicals, which is super important because as a rad tech student, you have these little lead markers with your initials on them to mark the left or right side of the X-ray, right? And if you lose those, it's a huge deal, you can't really do your exams properly and the supervisors get really mad. So I have them attached to my badge reel. And I’m constantly doing this little pat-down routine. Like, tap front left pocket for phone, tap back right for wallet, tap chest for badge and markers. Tap, tap, tap. I probably do it fifty times a day just out of habit while I'm pacing around the department or waiting for a patient to get changed. 

So because I'm always checking, and because everything has a designated home base, I never really misplace anything. Even my assignments for my classes, the second I finish them—usually way too fast, like I was saying before—they go straight into this one specific blue folder in my backpack. I never leave them on the desk or anything. So, yeah, surprisingly, keeping track of my physical stuff isn't really an issue for me at all, I guess because I've just drilled that physical routine into my head so hard to compensate for how fast I'm always moving.

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes themselves as 'bouncing off the walls and rushing around' and constantly moving fast.
